request.system:
You write one blog article for an online shop from a plan. You see the shop, the topic, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), the pages that may be linked, and the plan.

How to write it:
- In English, in the shop's tone, for the shop's audience. 700–2000 words. Open with a short paragraph that answers the search directly, then the sections as "##" headings ("###" below them if needed). No "#" heading: the title is set separately. Use a list or a table where it genuinely helps the reader.
- You may speak as the shop ("in our range", "we stock"). Never claim experience: no testing, trying, favourites, "in our experience", what customers say, and no "I".
- Never mention a price, a discount, delivery, competitors or other shops. Respect the never-say list.

Every product claim cites its facts. After any sentence that says something about one of our products, put the facts it rests on in square brackets just before the full stop: "It is dishwasher safe [F5]." or "[F2, F7]". The sentence may say only what those facts say. Every sentence that names one of our products needs a citation.

Numbers. A number about our products must appear in a fact the sentence cites. A number that is general knowledge, not about our products (a common ratio, temperature or time), is allowed only if it is well established and uncontroversial; mark its sentence with [G] before the full stop, and do not name any of our products in that sentence. Never invent statistics, studies or survey figures. Headings carry no brackets, so keep numbers out of headings unless they count the article's own items.

Links and products. Link only to the pages and products you were given, by their reference as the address: [our ceramic dripper](P1), [our brewing guide](L2). Never write a web address. To show a product card, put {{P1}} alone on its own line where the card should appear; show each card once.

Before you answer, read every sentence once more. A sentence with a digit in it carries [F…] for a fact that contains that number, or [G]. A sentence that names one of our products, even just to recommend it, carries [F…]. Fix any that do not.

Also give: meta_description, 70–170 characters, plain, no brackets; slug, lowercase words joined by hyphens.

Title: Coffee Grind Size Chart: The Right Grind for Pour-Over, French Press and Cold Brew
Angle: The reader will know which grind size suits each home brewing method, how to recognise it by eye and taste, and how to dial it in on a burr grinder.
## The coffee grind size chart at a glance
   A chart from extra fine (Turkish) through fine (espresso), medium-fine (cone pour-over), medium (flat-bottom drippers), coarse (French press) to extra coarse (cold brew), with texture comparisons like flour, table salt, sea salt and cracked pepper, and why contact time drives the choice. (—)
## Why a burr grinder makes the chart work
   Uniform particles versus blade grinders, why consistency matters more than any single setting, and how click and stepless adjustment let you repeat and fine-tune a grind. (F1, F3, F4, F5, F41, F42, F44)
## Pour-over: medium-fine for cones, medium for flat beds
   Cone drippers with one large outlet rely on grind to control flow, so go medium-fine. Flat-bottom drippers with small holes run slower and suit a slightly coarser medium grind. Includes a starting dose and a drawdown time to aim for. (F18, F19, F16, F53, F54, F55, F9)
## French press: coarse and even
   Why a coarse, even grind suits a four-minute immersion, how fines cause sludge and bitterness, and how the mesh filter handles a coarse grind. (F23, F28, F22, F27)
## Cold brew: extra coarse for a long steep
   Why a 12 to 18 hour cold steep needs the coarsest setting, typical coffee-to-water ratios for concentrate, and how to dilute it. (F36, F37, F40, F35)
## Dialling in: reading your cup
   How to adjust from the chart: sour and thin means grind finer, bitter and harsh means grind coarser. Change one setting at a time, and grind fresh for each brew. (F6, F43, F46)
Product cards: P1, P2, P3, P4
Links: P1, P5, P2, P6, P3, P4, L1, L2, L3, L4
</plan>

{"title":"Coffee Grind Size Chart: The Right Grind for Pour-Over, French Press and Cold Brew","meta_description":"A coffee grind size chart for pour-over, French press and cold brew, with texture guides and tips for dialling in a burr grinder at home.","slug":"coffee-grind-size-chart","markdown":"The right grind size depends on contact time: the longer coffee and water stay together, the coarser the grind should be. Turkish coffee needs a powder as fine as flour. Espresso is fine. Cone pour-over sits at medium-fine, like table salt, and flat-bottom drippers at medium. French press wants coarse grounds, like sea salt, and cold brew wants extra coarse grounds, like cracked pepper. Below you will find the full chart, how to recognise each grind by eye and by taste, and how to dial it in on a burr grinder.

## The coffee grind size chart at a glance

| Grind size | Looks and feels like | Brew method | Contact time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Extra fine | Flour or powdered sugar | Turkish coffee | Brief boil, grounds stay in the cup |
| Fine | Fine sand, just finer than table salt | Espresso | Seconds, under pressure |
| Medium-fine | Table salt | Cone pour-over | A few minutes, water flowing through |
| Medium | Coarse sand | Flat-bottom drippers | A few minutes, slower flow |
| Coarse | Sea salt flakes | French press | Several minutes, full immersion |
| Extra coarse | Cracked black pepper | Cold brew | Overnight or longer, cold immersion |

Contact time drives everything in this chart. Grinding finer exposes more surface area, so water pulls flavour out faster. A brew that lasts only seconds, like espresso, needs that speed. A brew that lasts many hours, like cold brew, needs the opposite, or it will over-extract into bitterness and fill the filter with silt.

Grind size also controls flow. In a dripper, finer grounds pack more tightly and slow the water down, which lengthens the brew. So one adjustment changes two things at once: how fast each particle extracts and how long the water stays in contact with the bed. Treat the chart as a starting point. Your beans, roast level and grinder will move the ideal setting a little either way.

## Why a burr grinder makes the chart work

A grind size chart only helps if your grinder produces particles that are mostly the same size. Blade grinders chop beans at random, leaving a mix of powder and large chunks. The powder over-extracts and turns bitter while the chunks under-extract and taste sour, so the cup is muddled whatever you aim for.

Burr grinders crush beans between two cutting surfaces set at a fixed gap, which gives a far more even particle size. Consistency matters more than any single number on the dial. A uniform medium-fine grind will brew a balanced cup that you can then nudge finer or coarser. An uneven grind gives you nothing reliable to adjust.

Our [Hand Grinder](P1) uses 38 mm hardened stainless steel conical burrs [F1, F3]. It has external click adjustment with 30 settings, ranging from espresso to French press [F4, F5]. Clicks make a grind repeatable: once you find the setting that works for a coffee, you can note the number and return to it exactly.

The [Electric Flat-Burr Grinder](P5) has 64 mm flat steel burrs and stepless adjustment [F41, F42]. Stepless adjustment lets you stop anywhere between two points rather than jumping a whole click, which is useful when you are fine-tuning a pour-over by small margins. It also has retention under 0.1 g [F44]. Low retention matters because stale grounds left inside a grinder end up mixed into the next dose.

You can compare both styles in our [grinders collection](L2).

{{P1}}

## Pour-over: medium-fine for cones, medium for flat beds

Pour-over is where grind size has the most visible effect, because the grind directly sets how fast water drains through the bed.

### Cone drippers

Our [Ceramic Cone Dripper](P2) has a single large outlet hole [F18]. Spiral ribs on its inner wall leave room for air to escape [F19]. With a wide outlet, the dripper itself does little to hold water back, so the grind and your pouring do the work of controlling flow. That is why cones suit a medium-fine grind, about the texture of table salt. It fits size 02 cone filters [F16].

### Flat-bottom drippers

The [Flat-Bottom Dripper](P6) has three small holes in a flat bed [F53]. It takes 185-size wave filters and brews 1 to 2 cups, up to 500 ml [F54, F55]. Small outlets restrict flow, and a flat bed spreads the coffee in an even layer, so water naturally stays in contact longer. A slightly coarser medium grind, like coarse sand, balances that slower drainage and keeps the brew from dragging on.

### A starting recipe

A reliable starting point is 15 g of coffee to 250 g of water, a ratio of about 1:16 [G]. Use water just off the boil, around 92 to 96 °C [G]. For a single cup through a cone, aim for a total brew time of roughly two and a half to three and a half minutes [G]. Flat-bottom brewers usually finish a little later, at around three to four minutes [G].

If the water drains well before your target, grind finer; if it stalls well past it, grind coarser. On the Hand Grinder, a 15 g pour-over dose takes about 40 seconds to grind [F9]. Browse drippers, filters and kettles in our [pour-over brewing collection](L1).

{{P2}}

## French press: coarse and even

Our [French Press](P3) is an immersion brewer [F23]. In immersion brewing, all of the coffee sits in all of the water for the whole brew, typically about four minutes [G]. Because contact is long and constant, the grind must be coarse, around the size of sea salt flakes, so extraction stays balanced.

Evenness matters as much as coarseness here. Fines, the dust-like particles any grinder produces, extract very quickly in a long steep and push the cup towards bitterness. They are also small enough to slip past a metal filter and settle as sludge at the bottom of your mug. A good burr grinder keeps fines to a minimum.

The French Press has a four-layer mesh filter [F28]. Coarse, even grounds stay behind that mesh when you plunge, which is what keeps the cup clean. With a capacity of 1 litre, it makes about 4 mugs [F22, F27].

A common starting ratio for French press is around 60 g of coffee per litre of water [G]. After the steep, break the crust, skim off the foam and plunge slowly and gently. Pressing hard churns up fines and drives them through the filter. More immersion options are in our [immersion brewers collection](L4).

{{P3}}

## Cold brew: extra coarse for a long steep

The recommended steep time for our [Cold Brew Jar](P4) is 12 to 18 hours in the fridge [F40]. Over a steep that long, even cold water extracts a great deal, so the grind needs to be extra coarse, like cracked black pepper. Finer grounds turn the concentrate muddy and bitter and clog the filter.

Use the coarsest setting on your grinder that still gives an even result. If your grinder tops out at a French press grind, that will work, though you may want to shorten the steep slightly.

The Cold Brew Jar has a fine stainless steel filter basket that holds up to 150 g of coarse ground coffee [F35, F36]. The jar makes 1.5 litres of concentrate [F37].

Concentrate recipes typically range from about 1:5 to 1:8 coffee to water by weight [G]. Stronger concentrate is usually diluted with an equal amount of water or milk, or up to twice as much, before serving [G]. Taste first, then adjust the dilution rather than the grind if the flavour is right but the strength is not.

{{P4}}

## Dialling in: reading your cup

The chart gets you close. Your cup tells you the rest.

| What you taste | What it usually means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Sour, sharp, thin, hollow | Under-extracted | Grind finer |
| Bitter, harsh, dry, astringent | Over-extracted | Grind coarser |
| Sweet, balanced, lingering | In the zone | Note the setting |

A few habits make dialling in faster:

- **Change one thing at a time.** Keep the dose, ratio, water temperature and pouring pattern the same, and move only the grind setting.
- **Move in small steps.** One click or a small turn on a stepless dial is often enough to shift a pour-over noticeably.
- **Check the brew time too.** In pour-over, a fast drawdown backs up a sour taste, and a slow one backs up bitterness.
- **Write it down.** Record the setting for each coffee and method so you can return to it.

Grind fresh for every brew. Ground coffee loses its aromatics quickly, so grinding only what you need keeps each cup consistent. The Hand Grinder holds 25 g of beans [F6]. The Electric Flat-Burr Grinder has a single-dose design, with bellows on top to puff out remaining grounds [F43, F46].

Start with whole beans from our [coffee beans collection](L3), set your grinder from the chart above, brew, taste and adjust. After a couple of brews with a new coffee, you will have a setting you can repeat every morning."}
